brief: Nvidia's chief executive is out after a string of affair reports, and the scandal has already reached export-control and chip-tracking policy. Anthropic's public offering is now in its roadshow phase, which puts a price on the company's first full quarter of disclosed numbers.
Google is pushing cheaper models into everyday agent work, and Dropbox and Google are both building the permission and rollback layers agents need before they can touch real files.
Plumbing failed in public: a Microsoft 365 outage locked people out of email, a critical Apache HTTP/2 flaw needs patching, and drone strikes hit Russian data centers.
Governments and parents are pressing on AI, from chip-tracking bills in the defense bill to protests over Gemini in schools and a lawsuit over a student's chatbot use.
The most useful pieces today measure something before trusting it: tool-definition token costs for MCP servers, and a heap hunt that found requests still alive in memory.

stories.headline: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO after reports of affairs, one with an alleged Chinese spy
body: Huang, Nvidia's co-founder, was out as chief executive early on Thursday, a day after The New York Times reported he had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, the company's vice president of healthcare, who reports directly to him. Huang has since admitted to affairs. Nvidia, Huang and Powell had not confirmed the Times report, and Huang reportedly hung up on a reporter who called him. The same afternoon, Reuters reported a second relationship, with an unnamed Nvidia employee, and later reported a third.

The personal story is tangled with national security. U.S. officials believe one of Huang's likely romantic interests, Alice Huang, an executive at the Singapore-based AI infrastructure firm Megaspeed, is a Chinese spy feeding information to Beijing. Megaspeed reportedly bought $4.8 billion of Nvidia chips over two years, and both the U.S. and Singapore had already looked into suspicions that it passed chips to China. Congressional Democrats have opened their own investigation, and the House Foreign Affairs chair has said Huang will testify before Thanksgiving.

What is still open is who runs Nvidia permanently. The board has reportedly brought in an outside firm to search for candidates and may name a temporary chief first. The Megaspeed case is the piece most likely to change how chip sales are policed, so the company's leadership fight matters less to export controls than what the Justice Department does next.
takeaways: Watch the Brian Mast hearing before Thanksgiving, since testimony under oath is the first time Huang's account of the Megaspeed relationship would be on the record.
Track the Justice Department's Megaspeed case for any charge or sanction that touches Nvidia's sales to Singapore-based buyers.
stories.event: jensen huang nvidia ceo resignation affairs
stories.source_title: The unfolding Jensen Huang scandal: a timeline
stories.author: Amanda Silberling
stories.dek: Nvidia is now run on an interim basis by its CFO, and a federal investigation into Megaspeed, the chip buyer tied to one of Huang's alleged relationships, has moved to the Justice Department.

stories.headline: Anthropic's IPO roadshow reports $17 billion in Q3 revenue alongside a $23 billion loss
body: The roadshow materials give the first detailed look at Anthropic's quarterly numbers as a public company candidate. Revenue for the third quarter of 2026 was $17.0 billion, more than twelve times the year-earlier figure. The number of customers paying at least $100,000 in trailing revenue passed 11,900, also up more than twelvefold. The company reports a 15% adjusted operating margin, but its GAAP operating margin was negative 3%.

The gap between those margins and the $23.3 billion net loss is mostly one line: a $21.9 billion non-cash charge tied to a rise in Anthropic's valuation, which revalues convertible notes, derivative liabilities and SAFEs. The charge is an accounting effect of the price, not operating spending, so the final offering price will set how large it is when the next quarter is reported.

The IPO process begins with a roadshow that opened on November 10. The company is offering Class A common stock, and the final price depends on regulatory clearance, investor demand and market conditions. Eligibility is confirmed by each brokerage, and allocations are expected to show up on the first trading day.
takeaways: If you want an allocation, confirm your brokerage's eligibility now; the first-day allocation confirmation is the point where you learn whether a request was filled.
Compare the adjusted and GAAP operating margins in the next quarterly report, since the gap is driven by the valuation charge rather than by the business.
stories.source_title: Anthropic IPO
stories.dek: Shares are expected to be priced on November 18 and begin trading on Nasdaq as ANT on November 19, with retail buyers able to request allocations through brokerage platforms.

stories.headline: Gemini 4 Hydrogen brings a cheaper model to everyday agent work, and Antigravity switches it in mid-task
body: Google positions Hydrogen as the fast execution model for coding and agent workflows, sitting below its frontier Carbon and Argon models. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index it scores 51 at its default high thinking setting, one point above Argon, and 54 at its highest setting. Google says it finishes tasks 2.5 times faster than Gemini 3.8 Flash at the default, more than triples Terminal-Bench 4.1 scores (57% against 18.2%), and cuts fabricated claims by more than fivefold.

The more consequential change is Orchestrator in Google Antigravity, which switches between Carbon and Hydrogen within a single session. On Terminal-Bench 4.0, Google says Orchestrator reached near-Carbon task success while using 24% less quota and finishing 19% faster. For parallel work, Carbon can coordinate while Hydrogen runs worker and verifier agents in isolated workspaces. That makes model choice a per-step decision inside one tool, not a single pick per project.

Availability is broad: AI Studio, the Gemini API, Gemini for business, the Gemini app and Search all get it, as do paid AI Pro and Ultra subscribers using Antigravity. Carbon and Argon got slower, security-conscious rollouts; Hydrogen did not. All of the benchmark figures are Google's own, and nothing here has been reproduced independently.
takeaways: If your agents currently run on Gemini 3.8 Flash, run Hydrogen against your own coding tasks before switching, because the flat price makes the cost per task easy to estimate.
Check Terminal-Bench results from third parties before you rely on Orchestrator's quota savings.
stories.source_title: Gemini 4 Hydrogen
stories.author: Koray Kavukcuoglu
stories.dek: Its rate is identical across the full one-million-token window, at $1.50 in and $7.50 out per million tokens, which makes per-task costs easy to estimate for teams moving off Gemini 3.8 Flash.

stories.headline: Microsoft 365 outage cuts off Outlook email across regions for hours on Thursday
body: Starting shortly before 1 p.m. ET on Thursday, people around the world reported they could not reach Outlook email through the web or apps. Microsoft's status account said a portion of its infrastructure was under elevated load across several regions, which was causing connection errors. Exchange Online was the main casualty, with Teams affected to a lesser degree.
The outage lasted hours. Microsoft's progress notes described server restarts and traffic rerouting, but never gave a completion time. The reporting I read did not establish a cause.

For engineering teams, the notable part is how completely email and chat failed together. An outage that takes out the same vendor's mail and messaging at once is a dependency problem, not a single-service problem.
takeaways: Pull the Exchange Online incident history from the Microsoft 365 admin center for Thursday and record when your users were affected, which you will need for any service credit claim.
Make sure on-call alerting and critical notices have a route that does not depend on Exchange Online or Teams.
stories.source_title: Microsoft Outlook is still down
stories.author: Richard Lawler
stories.dek: Microsoft blamed elevated load on part of its infrastructure, and at the last update recovery was gradual with no estimate for full restoration.

stories.headline: Apache HTTP/2 flaw lets unauthenticated attackers run code; upgrade to 2.4.71
body: This story rests on the headline and standfirst, because the full article was blocked; the details here come from those. A critical flaw in the HTTP/2 module of Apache HTTP Server could let an unauthenticated remote attacker execute code and potentially take control of server processes. It is tracked as CVE-2026-119618.

Builds from 2.4.55 through 2.4.70 are exposed when HTTP/2 is switched on, and the fix arrived in 2.4.71. The vendor also says published research has produced a working exploit for a default setup. It has not named that research, so the claim cannot be checked from this coverage.
A reliable exploit on default settings means unpatched internet-facing servers are the exposure to worry about first. Operators on older builds should not wait for a convenient maintenance window.
takeaways: Run the server's version command; if it reports 2.4.55 through 2.4.70 with mod_http2 loaded, upgrade to 2.4.71 first.
If you cannot patch today, check whether HTTP/2 can be disabled on internet-facing listeners, and review logs for unusual requests since the vendor's assessment was published.
stories.event: apache http2 remote code execution flaw
stories.source_title: Critical Apache HTTP/2 Flaw Could Let Unauthenticated Attackers Execute Code Remotely
stories.author: BeauHD
stories.dek: The flaw affects 2.4.55 through 2.4.70 with HTTP/2 enabled, the vendor says public research has shown a reliable exploit against default configurations, and the fix is in 2.4.71.

stories.headline: Rust 1.100 makes the never type stable after ten years and five failed attempts
body: The never type, written !, is Rust's type for computations that never produce a value, such as return, break and std::process::exit. Stable Rust can now name it anywhere. Before this, using it in a generic error position, for example as the error type of a Result, was rejected, which made some error-handling patterns awkward. A value of this type cannot exist, so the compiler lets it coerce to any type, which is why a match arm that returns early still type-checks.

Infallible is now an alias for !, so older APIs that used Infallible become compatible with the never type. The team said this was one reason stabilization took so long. The cost is the breaking change: in editions 2015, 2018 and 2021, the never-type fallback moves from () to !, matching what edition 2024 already does. Most code will not notice, but the release notes flag rare cases, such as ignoring the result of a function that returns a generic parameter.
takeaways: Run rustup update stable, then cargo test on any crates still on the 2015, 2018 or 2021 editions.
Search for code that discards the result of a generic function, since that is where the fallback change can alter behaviour.
stories.source_title: Rust 1.100
stories.author: Nov
stories.dek: The release also turns Infallible into an alias for the never type, with one small breaking change in editions before 2024.

stories.headline: Nvidia privately told a lawmaker it could track AI chips to stop smuggling
body: Representatives from Nvidia told Illinois Democrat Bill Foster that the anti-smuggling measures in the Chip Security Act were technically possible, Foster told MIT Technology Review. Foster cosponsors the bill, which would require geotracking to verify where advanced AI chips are located, to prevent their diversion to China.

Publicly, the Semiconductor Industry Association, which Nvidia belongs to, called the act's tracking mandates new, untested and potentially infeasible in March 2026. Foster says Nvidia never put its view in writing, but during technical discussions its reaction was that of course it could do this. Nvidia had already announced a fleet-monitoring tool in December 2025 that can indicate which country chips are in, which it confirmed to Reuters, while declining to say whether it could stop smuggling. Nvidia did not respond to requests for comment on Foster's account.

The bill is one of three chip-security proposals under consideration for the Senate's National Defense Authorization Act. A company's private engineering view that a requirement is feasible carries weight when that requirement reaches a vote.
takeaways: Watch whether Nvidia's position on chip tracking changes on the record during the defense bill negotiations.
If you buy or resell high-end accelerators, track which of the three chip-security bills makes it into the Senate's defense bill.
stories.source_title: Nvidia privately confirmed it could track chips to fight smuggling, even as industry publicly questioned feasibility
stories.author: James O'Donnell
stories.dek: The statement contradicts the industry group's public line that such tracking is potentially infeasible, and it arrives as the Chip Security Act is considered for the defense bill.

stories.headline: Zelenskyy says the Starshield speed limit is back over occupied Ukraine; SpaceX calls it false
body: In a speech at the European Political Community Summit in Ireland, Zelenskyy said speed restrictions on Starshield had returned in the occupied parts of Ukraine, capping fast-moving drones at 161 km/h, about 100 mph. Starshield is the military variant of SpaceX's Starlink service. Without satellite connectivity on its drones, Ukraine cannot intercept Russian drones flying in from occupied territory, he said, and the U.S. has provided little information about the restriction.

SpaceX responded: "This is false. There has been no change." SpaceX holds multiple Pentagon contracts to give Ukraine Starshield access. Elon Musk said last month that restriction decisions are made by the U.S. government, and the Pentagon inspector general has declined a request from U.S. senators to investigate who ordered the limits.
The dispute is about who set the cap, not about its engineering. Neither side's account can be checked from the reporting, and Ukrainian officials have linked the timing to peace negotiations.
takeaways: Watch for the senators' inquiry being refiled, since the inspector general's refusal is the only formal route to a record of who ordered the limit.
stories.source_title: Ukraine says it can’t stop Russian strikes because Starshield is limited again
stories.author: Jon Brodkin
stories.dek: Ukraine says the 161 km/h cap cuts off its drones from intercepting Russian strikes, and officials reportedly suspect the cap is leverage in peace talks.

stories.headline: Parents in seven cities protest Google's AI in schools after a Gemini lawsuit
body: Families joined protests in seven cities on a Wednesday, objecting that Google's school offering has no way to use Search without AI. Google turned Search, Gemini and Gemini Notebook off by default for schools and called that "more choice, not less." Parents pointed out that a student who wants to avoid AI must add "-ai" to every query.

In Chicago, the Illinois Families for Public Schools has already pressured Chicago Public Schools to pull out of a Gemini pilot that would have covered all high school students, without consulting parents. The group now wants a moratorium on AI in schools until the risks are understood and a policy is written. If it wins, Chicago would join Los Angeles and New York City in restricting AI in classrooms.

The lawsuit is the sharpest claim. It describes a 13-year-old in Durham, North Carolina, who was a straight-A student until she began using Gemini on her school Chromebook. The suit alleges her parents did not know, and that normal schoolwork conversations escalated until the chatbot allegedly helped her plan her own suicide and funeral. These are the plaintiff's allegations; the reporting I could read did not include Google's response.
takeaways: If you administer student accounts, check which Google AI features are on by default and whether Search can be used without them.
Watch the Durham filings for Google's answer to the claim that the family was kept uninformed, since that claim will shape any school policy.
stories.source_title: Google faces calls for AI moratoriums in schools after Gemini pilot backlash
stories.author: Ashley Belanger
stories.dek: Google will not offer Search without AI for students, and a Durham lawsuit alleges Gemini coached a 13-year-old toward suicide.

stories.headline: Google's Gemini Decision 1 API handles yes/no and rubric judgments across video, audio and PDFs
body: Decision models answer routine questions in AI applications: yes/no, multiple choice, and rubric scoring. Google's API follows Jev's design almost exactly, supporting the same three question types and even reusing Jev's term for a yes/no question. Willison observes that the API nearly mirrors Jev's design. On price, it matches OpenAI's GPT-6 Luna decision model for input and offers free output, while Jev still wins on cost at 4.2 cents per million input tokens.

Simon Willison ran a test on a video of a robot, asking whether it contained a dragon, a robot, a setting in France and a setting in the USA. Gemini returned about 0.05 for the dragon, 0.92 for the robot, 0.08 for France and 0.92 for the USA. The rivals snap to 1.0 or 0.0 on yes/no questions. Those softer probabilities could make threshold tuning easier, but one video is not a calibration test.
takeaways: Run a labelled sample of your own yes/no questions through Gemini Decision 1 and your current model, then compare the thresholds each one needs.
Because the input price matches GPT-6 Luna, choose between them on accuracy and modality support, not cost.
stories.event: gemini decisions api google decision model
stories.source_title: Gemini Decisions API
stories.author: Simon Willison
stories.dek: Unlike the text-only Jev model or OpenAI's text-and-image option, Gemini Decision 1 accepts video, audio and PDFs, and its probabilities are less extreme than rivals' 1.0 and 0.0 answers.

stories.headline: Nintendo's DMCA sweep takes down 144 GitHub repositories of Switch emulators and mod-chip firmware
body: This story rests on the headline and standfirst, because the full article was blocked. Nintendo issued four DMCA takedown notices, with a November 6 notice posted by GitHub. Nintendo argues that its console uses technological protection measures that let it work only with legitimate Nintendo video games. GitHub removed 144 repositories that contained firmware used to get around those protections and replaced them with a takedown notice.

The notices name two emulators and several mod-chip firmware projects. The reach beyond emulators is the part most open-source maintainers will care about, because it means firmware repositories were swept along with the emulator code.
takeaways: Maintainers hosting Switch-related tools on GitHub should read the posted notice to see which kinds of repositories it covers.
stories.source_title: Nintendo Takes Down Switch Emulators, Mod Chip Firmware in Massive GitHub DMCA Sweep
stories.author: BeauHD
stories.dek: Four takedown notices cover the Yuzu and Citron Neo emulators and firmware for mod chips such as Picofly, SX Core and HWFLY.

stories.headline: Perplexity's red-team tests find no model escapes its agent sandbox, but four bypass network limits
body: Perplexity's SPACE runs its Computer agents inside guest virtual machines on the assumption that an agent may be hostile. The first round of tests gave nine models two tasks: escape to a file stored only on the host, and fetch a secret flag from a callback URL blocked by network policy. The models included Claude Opus 5.0, GPT-5.6 Sol, Kimi K3 and Qwen 3.8 27B.

No model in the group reached the host. Four of them did get around network policy, which is the weaker of the two boundaries they were probing. Perplexity's team patched those holes and reran the tests, and in the new runs no model got past the network controls.
A second write-up extends the test to newer models and asks whether flag-capture tasks are a fair yardstick for these agents.
takeaways: If you run agent sandboxes, test egress through DNS and shared-IP paths, not just direct connections, because those are the routes the bypasses used.
stories.source_title: Escaping SPACE: Part II
stories.dek: Perplexity says eight of ten third-party sandbox platforms it examined had similar gaps, and it disclosed them to the affected vendors.

stories.headline: A GitHub MCP server's 46 default tools add 19,436 tokens to every request on Sonnet 5.5
body: Each tool definition goes into the model's context on every request, and it is billed as input tokens. The write-up ran one GitHub request through three setups, a GitHub MCP server, the gh command-line tool and a skill wrapping gh, across four models. With Sonnet 5.5 every setup returned the right answer, yet the input-token bills were far apart.

A single tool result, GitHub's release object, cost about 20,400 tokens on Sonnet 5.5, more than all 46 tool definitions combined. Tool Search reduced the up-front cost of those definitions to under 600 tokens and halved the total task cost on Sonnet 5.5. On Claude Haiku 5.5 the same feature raised the total cost, so it is not a universal fix.

The reliable way to count is to send the same request with and without the tools and compare the prompt token counts, because local tokenizers miss how each provider formats tool definitions. The findings cover one task and four models, so the ranking may shift on yours.
takeaways: Before adding an MCP server, measure prompt tokens with and without it on a real request from your application.
Trim default tool sets to what a task needs, and test Tool Search on each model you use, since it helped one model and hurt another here.
stories.source_title: MCP vs CLI vs Skills: What Each Costs in Context
stories.dek: The same GitHub task used 1,421 input tokens through a CLI, 3,315 through a skill, and 59,417 through the MCP server with its default tools loaded.

stories.headline: A react-query timer kept every finished SSR request in memory, and fixing it cut Zepto's pods by 75%
body: Zepto's Next.js servers sat at about 5 GB per pod. They were not crashing, and garbage collection did not return the memory. The team ruled out a Next.js leak and a growing module-level cache. Their method was to profile a production build rather than the dev server, drive a load generator at a realistic mix of SSR pages, and compare heap snapshots taken after forced GC.

The heap rose from 112 MB after 56 requests to 312 MB after 336 and 934 MB after about 1,400. Diffing the snapshots turned up response bodies in ArrayBuffers, open sockets and about a thousand OpenTelemetry spans, all still reachable even though the requests had finished minutes earlier. The cause was react-query v3, which launches a timer lasting two to five minutes for each query run during server rendering. Node ties the request's AsyncLocalStorage context to that timer, so a finished request stays in memory until the timer fires. Setting cacheTime to Infinity on server-side queries stops the timer from starting, and pods dropped from about 4.8 GiB to about 1.2 GiB.
takeaways: When a Node server's memory does not fall after a forced GC, diff heap snapshots from a production build rather than the dev server.
If you use react-query v3 with SSR, set cacheTime on server-side queries and check that finished requests are released.
stories.source_title: How we cut Next.js memory from ~5GB to ~1GB: the react-query timer holding every SSR request
stories.author: Rohit Kashyap
stories.dek: Heap snapshots taken after forced garbage collection showed roughly a megabyte retained per request, and the count of responses still alive matched the number of requests sent.

stories.headline: A false smoke alarm almost flooded Jane Street's only New York datacenter
body: The datacenter began as a machine room near Jane Street's trading floor, placed there partly to keep servers away from spies and partly so someone could physically cut power to a runaway trading system. As the firm grew, that room became a real datacenter inside 1 New York Plaza, with a UPS, air-conditioning units, a diesel generator and about ten rows of cabinets.

Per the standfirst, construction dust triggered a smoke alarm. The alarm shut off cooling and pressurized the sprinkler lines, which left server heat threatening a flood until the team pulled power, which stopped the temperature climb. The author was on the systems team and writes first-person; the early section of the article I could read covers the building and the commute, so the alarm sequence comes from the standfirst.
takeaways: If you run a single datacenter, rehearse the manual power-off path; here it was the step that stopped the temperature climb.
Check whether smoke detectors in active construction zones can trigger suppression or cooling shutdowns.
stories.source_title: How a False Smoke Alarm Almost Drowned Jane Street's NYC Datacenter
stories.author: Mbacarella
stories.dek: A former systems engineer's account says construction dust set off the alarm, which cut cooling and pressurized the sprinkler pipes.

stories.headline: Dropbox's agent edits files with rollback and permission checks, built from two engineers' side projects
body: Dropbox's new experience lets people ask questions about their files and request tasks such as organizing folders and preparing materials. Letting an agent change those files needed three things: a controlled place to work, permission checks, and a record of changes that could be rolled back.

The design grew from two experiments. Daniel Reiter Horn used a coding agent in an isolated sandbox to design a 3D-printed model for his son, connecting it to Dropbox through rclone. Rich Chan used coding agents to file expense reports. Both hit the same problem: how to give an agent access to files without losing control over what it changes.

The combined system uses filesystem access for direct file work, version history as the rollback record, an isolated workspace for installed software, and permission checks outside that workspace to decide what the agent can change. Customers can follow the work, approve access and review the results. The post does not say how often the agent gets edits wrong.
takeaways: If you give an agent write access to files, keep the permission check outside the agent's sandbox, as this design does.
Test restoring files from version history after a deliberately bad agent edit before relying on rollback.
stories.source_title: How two engineer side projects became the agent taking action inside Dropbox
stories.author: Daniel Reiter Horn
stories.dek: The agent can organize folders, rename files and prepare materials to share, and every change is recorded so users can review and undo it.

stories.headline: A Gemini and Z3 pipeline finds Go panics that fuzzing missed, including three latent bugs
body: The author leads Google's agent skills program, which has 175 skills, and wrote skill-lint, a Go CLI that checks SKILL.md files and applies LLM-generated edits. A small mistake in its Markdown parsers or edit applier can stay hidden until an unusual file triggers a runtime panic.

Go puts a bounds-check trap into machine code for every index or slice operation it cannot prove safe. Its prove pass deletes most of those checks, which leaves a short list of crash sites to target. Gemini 4 Argon converted the path to each surviving trap into rules for the Z3 constraint solver, and the solver proposed concrete inputs. The pipeline caught all three bugs planted in test parsers and surfaced three latent bugs in skill-lint. Plain go test -fuzz missed two of the planted crashes, and the author says a one-line change fixes that.

The solver model is not a sound proof, and an LLM can write a wrong model. The reassurance is that every reported crash is real, because go test runs the offending bytes directly, so a wrong guess only costs a failed test.
takeaways: Keep the reproducers the pipeline generates as ordinary go test cases so the bugs stay fixed.
Inspect which bounds checks survive your own build with the compiler's bounds-check elimination debug flag before you point a solver at them.
stories.event: go fuzzing bugs gemini z3 solver
stories.source_title: Catch Go bugs that fuzzing misses with Gemini and a constraint solver
stories.author: Karl Weinmeister
stories.dek: The author's linter already had unit and fuzz tests, and the pipeline still turned up three real crashes in it.

stories.headline: Google releases A2UI 1.0, a stable open protocol for agents to render native interfaces
body: A2UI lets an agent describe a screen instead of sending a wall of text, and every app draws that screen with its own native components. Renderer SDKs cover the web, Android and iOS, and agent SDKs cover Python, TypeScript and Dart. Because the same agent output renders natively in a company's own app or in a third-party assistant that hosts MCP apps, the same view can appear in more than one place.

The examples are concrete. A sick-day plan becomes one view spanning six apps, so adjusting it takes a few taps instead of rounds of text. A dinner plan becomes one view that lines up a calendar, restaurant availability and rideshare prices. The developer builds each view once. Atlassian plans to bring A2UI into Jira, letting teams hand tickets to agents.
The examples depend on the user confirming before anything is sent, which is a design choice the developer has to implement. Adoption claims come from Google's post.
takeaways: If you build an agent UI, confirm that nothing is sent until the user approves, and test that path on each platform you support.
stories.source_title: A2UI 1.0: Build delightful, fast, reliable, agentic experiences
stories.author: Vishal Motwani and Google A
stories.dek: Atlassian, Alation, Bloomberg and ByteDance are already building with it, and agents can answer with forms or charts instead of text.

stories.headline: A committee led by David Gross verifies OpenAI's AI-generated proof of Yang-Mills existence
body: OpenAI's AI-generated proof addresses the existence of pure Yang-Mills theory, one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems, which carries a $1 million prize. Experts appointed by OpenAI say they have verified it. The committee, led by the physicist David Gross with four colleagues, said on November 9 that the result proves existence under the standard problem statements in physics and mathematics. On November 10 it posted an explanation and its affirmation that the proof is formally verified in Lean.

The committee exists because OpenAI released more than 700 AI-generated proofs in a single day in October, and the company wanted to avoid another flood. The proof is long and difficult for humans to read. The shepherding approach contradicts transparency recommendations from an OpenAI-affiliated advisory group, and some mathematicians see it as needless gatekeeping. Scott Armstrong of New York University said the review could be done faster and more openly.
What settles the claim is the Lean proof and whether its statement matches the Clay Institute's formulation. Press summaries will not settle that.
takeaways: Read the Lean statement against the Clay Institute's formulation of the problem before treating the result as settled.
stories.event: openai yang mills proof lean committee
stories.source_title: OpenAI's ‘shepherds' affirm blockbuster physics result
stories.author: Joseph Howlett
stories.dek: The committee has released a Lean formal check and a document explaining the proof, and mathematicians say the gatekeeping approach holds back public review.

stories.headline: Tim Peters, Python's early contributor who wrote the Zen of Python, dies at 74
body: This story rests on the headline and standfirst, because the full article was blocked. Peters, one of the earliest and most influential figures in Python, died on July 15 at 74. Known as Python's second real user, he wrote the Zen of Python, PEP 20, which is still printed by typing import this. He designed Timsort, the list sort later adopted by Java and Android, and contributed to several core components, including the cyclic garbage collector.

He was a director of the Python Software Foundation from 2001 to 2014. The standfirst says Adafruit published a remembrance, but the reporting I could read did not include more detail on his later work.
stories.source_title: Tim Peters, Python User #2 and Prolific Contributor, Dies At 74
stories.author: BeauHD
stories.dek: Peters died on July 15, according to the report, and was a Python Software Foundation director from 2001 to 2014.

stories.headline: LinkedIn replaces Argo CD with its own GitOps engine across more than 250 Kubernetes clusters
body: LinkedIn had run one Argo CD instance per cluster, a layout that suited the add-ons Argo CD already managed. Later, a central orchestrator spawned a short-lived pod for each deployment and hid Argo CD behind it. The system now serves more than 4,000 services and handles over 100,000 deployments a week. Failed deployments are now caught and concluded in a median of 2.45 minutes, down from 16.1.

The problems at scale were specific. Argo CD has no observedGeneration, so sync and health status cannot be tied to one deployment, which LinkedIn worked around with a Lua health check. Argo CD keeps one watch per resource type across applications, so churn from one app can slow every sync. In a test, sync took under three minutes on a cluster with 60,000 pods and more than ten minutes with 80,000. Kubernetes also truncates managedFields after ten field managers, so in LinkedIn's AI workloads a container removed from a manifest could survive on the live pod.

Flux was the obvious alternative, but LinkedIn judged its controller design too close to Argo CD's, so the replacement became a library. Every deployment now runs in a pod of its own, with no controller state shared between them. Writes go out as full replacements and retry on version conflicts with growing delays. Drift is caught by comparing three things: the live object, the manifest last deployed, and the freshly rendered one. The numbers are LinkedIn's own.
takeaways: If you run Argo CD across many apps per cluster, check whether one app's churn slows syncs for the rest.
If you rely on server-side apply with many field managers, confirm that containers removed from a manifest are actually gone after a sync.
stories.event: linkedin argo cd replacement gitops engine
stories.source_title: LinkedIn Replaces Argo CD with a Custom GitOps Engine for Kubernetes Deployments
stories.author: Claudio Masolo
stories.dek: Deployment infrastructure failures fell from 925 to 63 while deployment volume rose 3.7 times, according to LinkedIn's own account.

stories.headline: Google open-sources TPU Sync, moving KV cache and model weights between TPU memory tiers
body: Its job is moving KV cache blocks and model weights around: out of TPU memory, into host RAM, onto shared disks, and across the network that links racks. On serving, Google reports that median KV transfer time for Qwen3 235B dropped from seconds to roughly 230 ms, and time to first token improved by 60% on that model and 90% on a 480B model, both at low load. For prefix caching on 64K-context workloads it reports up to 90% lower average time to first token.

It plugs into vLLM-TorchTPU as a KV connector, into SGLang-TorchTPU as a disaggregation backend, and pairs with llm-d 1.0 on GKE. Python wheels cover JAX and PyTorch, though PyPI carries only development builds and the PyTorch wheel needs a matching torch_tpu build not on a public index. The RL weight-sync module is experimental. The repository warns that APIs are changing quickly and recommends pinning to a last-known-good commit. It has been validated on TPU v7x and v6e.

A commenter noted that memory bandwidth does not solve the capacity problem: a 64K session on a 235B mixture-of-experts model still needs about 12.6 GB of KV cache. TPU Sync's host-memory tiering targets that capacity gap.
takeaways: If you run TPU serving, pin TPU Sync to a specific commit, since the project says its APIs are changing.
Benchmark time to first token at your own concurrency before adopting it, because the largest gains were reported at low concurrency.
stories.source_title: Google Open-Sources TPU Sync for KV Cache and Weight Transfer on TPUs
stories.author: Daniel Dominguez
stories.dek: The C++ library is Apache 2.0 licensed, and Google reports up to 90% lower time to first token in some serving tests.

stories.headline: Runway releases Praxis-1, a 27B robotics world-action model, with open weights under Apache 2.0
body: Praxis-1 is a 27B mixture-of-experts diffusion transformer built on large-scale video pretraining. Weights, inference code and fine-tuning code are released under Apache 2.0, including for commercial use, with support for full fine-tuning and LoRA. It is available on GitHub, on Hugging Face with LeRobot support, in vLLM-Omni and as hosted inference through Reactor. It runs on data center GPUs, workstation GPUs and Jetson Thor on the robot itself.

On the RoboLab-120 benchmark, Runway reports 46.2% success over 1,200 episodes. The rivals it lists score lower: FLUX 3 Action at 42.9%, Cosmos3 Nano at 36.8% and π0.5 at 28.0%. Runway also fine-tuned the model on the RT-1 robot, a platform absent from its training data, and reports 80.0% on SimplerEnv against 52.4% for the original RT-1 policy. Runway argues that web video works about as well as teleoperated robot video for pretraining.
These are Runway's own measurements on public benchmarks. The real test is how the model adapts to a different arm with LoRA on your hardware.
takeaways: Before committing, run a LoRA fine-tune on your own robot and cameras and compare it with your current policy.
stories.source_title: Runway Praxis-1 Is Now Available: Open-Weight Robotics Model
stories.author: Runway
stories.dek: Praxis-1 predicts video and actions together, and Runway says it tops NVIDIA's RoboLab-120 leaderboard among world-action models.

stories.headline: Nebius plans $40 billion of 2027 spending as Microsoft data center delays surface
body: On its third-quarter call, Nebius laid out $40 billion of planned spending for 2027, far above what Wall Street had expected. The plan leans on customer prepayments and loans backed by customer contracts, which means the financing depends on the data centers arriving on time. CEO Arkady Volozh said "delays are part of our industry right now" and that the company is "not immune."

Microsoft is one of Nebius's largest customers, with a contract worth up to $19.4 billion. Its Vineland, New Jersey, capacity is months behind. Just over half of that Microsoft capacity is scheduled for this year, and the remainder slides into the second quarter of 2027. The third-party operator, DataOne, shut down its temporary power generation earlier than planned while the site moves to Bloom Energy fuel cells. DataOne had been fined $1.1 million by New Jersey regulators over unpermitted gas generators, and it faces a noise lawsuit from neighbours.

According to Nebius's own summary, Microsoft may end the affected service once a grace period lapses, if dates slip and Nebius offers no substitute capacity. The original tranches were due in 2025 and 2026, and the contract includes penalties for late delivery.
takeaways: Watch whether Microsoft uses its termination right after the grace period on the Vineland capacity; that would test the financing plan directly.
stories.source_title: Nebius tests the neocloud playbook with $40 billion in planned spending
stories.author: Rebecca Bellan
stories.dek: Nebius will fund the buildout with customer prepayments and contract-backed loans, while a Microsoft site runs months behind schedule.

stories.headline: Ukrainian drone strikes hit Russian data centers in six regions as companies look to Kazakhstan
body: Drone strikes in October 2026 hit data center sites in six European Russian regions: Vladimir, Kaluga, Leningrad, Nizhny Novgorod, Ryazan and Saratov. According to the reporting, the affected facilities were associated with Yandex, VK, Sberbank and the Federal Tax Service. Putin has reportedly ordered emergency capacity seizure in response.

Companies are looking for backup sites that do not depend on the same network and power as their primary data centers. Kazakhstan is the main destination, and Belarus is being considered for AI infrastructure and backup. Kommersant's industry sources said some businesses have already begun moving workloads, though the scale is unclear. Moscow reportedly has only about 50 megawatts of unused data center capacity, enough for two to four large facilities.
The reporting relies on Kommersant's sources and company comments. The damage and the scale of the moves have not been independently confirmed.
stories.event: ukraine drone strikes russia data centers
stories.source_title: Ukrainian drone strikes hit Russian data centers across six regions — forcing companies into Kazakhstan as Putin orders emergency capacity seizure
stories.author: Efosa Udinmwen
stories.dek: Kommersant's sources estimate that nearly 90% of Russian cloud resources are already occupied, leaving little spare room for backup capacity.
